newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura scandal widens with political, bank twists.
newsitem.headline: Nomura scandal widens with political, bank twists.

text.p: A scandal centred on Japan's giant Nomura Securities took a twist with possible political repercussions on Tuesday when the chief government spokesman said three cabinet ministers held accounts at the brokerage.
And in another sign the scandal was widening, prosecutors on Tuesday entered the headquarters of one of Japan's top commercial banks, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB).
Top spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference that three cabinet members currently had "dealings" with Nomura, but said they were not getting preferential treatment.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters that neither he nor his immediate family had any dealings with Nomura. Several other cabinet ministers including Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka and Trade Minister Shinji Sato also denied any deals with the brokerage.

Analysts said the political aspect, for now at least, looked like a sideshow to the main drama of the widening racketeer payoff scandal at Japan's biggest brokerage as the nation begins its "Big Bang" financial deregulation.

Prosecutors last week arrested racketeer Ryuichi Koike and raided Nomura's head office and branches after taking in two former Nomura managing directors and another senior official suspected of violating Japan's Commercial Code and Securities and Exchange Law with payoffs to the "sokaiya" racketeer.
The investigation is focusing on whether other top Nomura executives were aware of the payoffs or whether, as the brokerage maintains, the officials involved acted on their own.

But prosecutors are also probing for signs of possible misdeeds linked to so-called "VIP accounts" set up for elite customers including bureaucrats and politicians. Nomura has denied preferential treatment was given to the estimated 8,000 to 9,000 holders of VIP accounts.

"I have checked with the three ministers and there is no connection (to the Nomura payoff scandal)," Kajiyama said. "The dealing were in government bonds and trust funds...none of which are instruments in which special favours could be granted." Kajiyama added, however, that his survey "did not dig deeply into the past", nor did it include family members.
A DKB spokesman, meanwhile, expressed regret over the situation and said it would cooperate with the investigation.

But the bank declined to comment on media reports that it had made questionable loans to Ryuichi Koike, arrested last week along with his younger brother Yoshinori Koike on suspicion of violating Japan's Commercial Code by taking some 50 million yen ($438,000) in illegal payments from Nomura.
The Commercial Code bans companies from making payments to "sokaiya", racketeers who typically extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt shareholder meetings.

On Monday, the Mainichi Shimbun reported that Ryuichi Koike owned about 20,000 DKB shares under various assumed names, and often attended DKB's shareholders' meeting as a "friendly sokaiya" -- one who uses his influence to stop "enemy sokaiya" from making extortion attempts at shareholders' meetings.

Japanese newspapers said DKB holds problem loans worth 7.5 billion yen ($65.7 million) linked to Koike, and that another financial firm with close ties with DKB has Koike-linked bad loans worth 1.2 billion yen ($10.5 million).
The reports said the elder Koike used the loans to buy 300,000 shares in each of Japan's top four brokerages including Nomura, and used the shares as collateral for the DKB loans.
Financial analysts said the fresh developments were embarrassing for DKB but might not hurt its business much.

For Nomura, already tainted by a 1991 scandal and now suffering from defections by corporate, government and individual clients, and facing probable stiff penalties and a court case, the outlook is grimmer.

Authorities have made clear they intend to mete out stiff punishment as a signal such misdeeds will not be tolerated anymore. Many analysts, however, still expect the brokerage to eventually weather the storm and survive as a key player in Japan's ever more deregulated and competitive markets.
Politicians, however, may escape serious fallout from the scandal, in part because so many members of Japan establishment are whispered to be on Nomura's VIP list, analysts said.

"Everyone knows there is a list...but everyone is covering each other and it is possible that we will never know who is on it because basically, the upper echelons are all included," said Chris Redl, a political analyst at ING Barings Securities.
